analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to sell standardized basic health coverage with guaranteed issue, and caps malpractice damages.
analysis.headline: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum introduced the bill with three Republican cosponsors in March 1992; the Senate Finance Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force insurance companies to offer a standardized 'BasiCare' health plan to small employers and, eventually, to everyone, with guaranteed acceptance, guaranteed renewal, limits on premiums, and capped out-of-pocket costs. It would expand community health centers and rural health staffing, let self-employed people deduct all health insurance costs, and set up a commission to design a national plan that would replace Medicaid after five years with vouchers for private BasiCare coverage, funded by a new payroll-based trust fund. It also caps malpractice awards and exempts hospital joint ventures from antitrust rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at small firms who today can be denied coverage or charged unaffordable rates would get guaranteed issue, guaranteed renewal, a required core benefit package, deductibles capped at $500 individual/$1,000 family, and out-of-pocket costs capped at $2,000/$3,000, with free preventive care for children and no cost-sharing for pregnancy care [S2][S3]. Self-employed people could deduct 100% of their health insurance costs instead of 25% [S2]. Low-income and rural communities would gain expanded community health centers and National Health Service Corps funding [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Insurers selling to small employers must offer a plan with Medicare-level core benefits, guaranteed issue, guaranteed renewability, preexisting-condition limits capped at 6 months, and premiums that vary by no more than 1.5 times the base rate, backed by a 35% excise tax on noncompliant insurers [S2][S3].

The bill authorizes $600 million a year for federally qualified health centers to reach medically underserved areas, plus $120 million a year for National Health Service Corps scholarships and loan repayment and tax credits of up to $1,000 a year for clinicians serving rural shortage areas [S2][S3].
Self-employed individuals could deduct 100% of health insurance costs, up from 25%, permanently [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would lose their ability to deny, drop, or steeply rate small-group coverage and would face a 35% excise tax for violations; doctors and their insurers would benefit from malpractice caps while injured patients would bear reduced compensation; all wage earners would fund the new BasiCare Trust Fund through a percentage of wages, and Medicaid would be wound down after five years [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Malpractice victims would have noneconomic damages capped at $250,000 per person and family regardless of the number of providers at fault, awards offset by other compensation they already receive, and attorneys' fees set by the court — the strongest good-faith tradeoff, meant to cut doctors' liability costs, is paid for by people harmed by negligent care [S2][S3].
Medicaid would be terminated after five years, with low-income people shifted to vouchers for private BasiCare premiums, a bet that subsidized private coverage will match what Medicaid provided [S2].
The bill preempts state insurance and malpractice laws, so states with stronger consumer protections or damage limits would see them overridden [S2][S3].
Federal preemption of state law and a ban on coverage duplicating BasiCare benefits would limit choices and override state consumer protections in some cases [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage protections for small-firm workers are substantial and mirror reforms that later became law. But the financing rests on a new wage-based tax, the phaseout of Medicaid in favor of vouchers was a genuine risk for the poorest beneficiaries, and the malpractice caps shift real costs onto injured patients. The bill is a serious attempt at universal-ish coverage with real tradeoffs, not a giveaway — though its antitrust carve-out for hospital joint ventures and its channeling of all coverage through private carriers entrench the insurance industry as the permanent gatekeeper of health care.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum (R-KS) introduced the BasiCare Health Access and Cost Control Act on March 12, 1992, during the health care reform debate [S1][S3][S5].
Three Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S2][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day — the last recorded action [S1][S5].
The bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and medical providers kept operating under the existing state-by-state rules, and employers kept the status quo; uninsured and underinsured Americans gained nothing. The bill's own ideas on guaranteed issue and renewability resurfaced years later in other legislation, but in 1992 the people it would have covered came out behind.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and providers kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, took no action to move the bill after it was referred

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so opposition was never measured; its sponsorship was entirely Republican — one sponsor and three Republican cosponsors — during a Democratic-controlled Congress [S2][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill forces every carrier to offer the standard BasiCare package, bans duplicative coverage, and eventually funnels Medicaid beneficiaries into private plans via vouchers — locking insurers in as the permanent delivery system — while stripping their power to deny, drop, or steeply rate small employers and imposing a 35% excise tax on violators [S2][S3].

Malpractice caps ($250,000 on noneconomic damages, collateral-source offsets, fee limits) plus rural tax credits and equipment expensing cut providers' liability exposure and costs — gains that come directly out of compensation for patients injured by negligent care [S2][S3].
The bill lets joint hospital ventures providing health services escape antitrust laws, reducing competitive pressure on hospital prices and consolidation [S2][S3].
New grants and $600 million a year in FQHC expansion funding would extend primary care to low-income and medically underserved populations [S2][S3].
Court-set fee limits and damage caps shrink malpractice suits; in this bill the trial bar's interest ran alongside injured patients' interest in full compensation.
